questions.question: What is a hazard in safety engineering terms?
options: A bug that always causes immediate failure
A requirement that guarantees full availability
A test case that proves a program correct
A security patch applied after deployment
A condition that could lead to an accident
questions.explanation: A hazard is a system condition with the potential to cause an accident.

questions.question: Risk is best described as which combination?
options: Combination of schedule and budget constraints
Combination of encryption and authentication methods
Combination of usability and performance metrics
Combination of hazard probability and severity
Combination of code style and documentation detail
questions.explanation: Risk combines how likely a hazard is and how severe the consequences could be.

questions.question: In hazard assessment, what does ALARP represent?
options: Risk eliminated by definition through compliance
Risk increased to maximize test coverage
Risk reduced as low as reasonably practicable
Risk accepted as large and unavoidable permanently
Risk ignored until after system deployment
questions.explanation: ALARP is a middle category where risk must be reduced as far as reasonably practicable.

questions.question: Which set lists core strategies for achieving safety?
options: Recruitment, promotion, compensation, retention
Refactoring, optimization, parallelization, caching
Feature growth, market fit, brand expansion
Hazard avoidance, hazard removal, damage limitation
Compilation, linking, loading, execution
questions.explanation: Safety strategies include avoiding hazards, detecting/removing hazards, and limiting damage when accidents occur.

questions.question: Fault tree analysis is best described as which technique?
options: Black-box analysis based on marketing surveys
Random sampling of inputs for usability tests
Graphical style guide for UML notation
Top-down deductive analysis from a hazard
Bottom-up inductive analysis from code units
questions.explanation: Fault tree analysis starts from a hazard and decomposes combinations of faults that could cause it.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a safety case?
options: Providing budget evidence that a system is cheap
Providing code evidence that a system is optimized
Providing structured evidence that a system is safe
Providing marketing evidence that a system is popular
Providing UI evidence that a system is attractive
questions.explanation: A safety case is a structured argument with evidence used to justify safety to regulators and stakeholders.

questions.question: Which pairing best matches technique to description?
options: Model checking is marketing; static analysis is sales
Model checking replaces tests; static analysis replaces specs
Model checking explores states; static analysis inspects code
Model checking is only manual; static analysis is only human
Model checking inspects code; static analysis explores states
questions.explanation: Model checking explores possible states for property violations, while static analysis examines source code for faults.

questions.question: What does ROCOF measure in reliability engineering?
options: Chance a demand fails at the time of request
Rate at which failures occur during operation
Total number of lines of code in system
Average time needed to repair after failure
Fraction of time the system is operational
questions.explanation: ROCOF is the rate of occurrence of failures during system operation.

questions.question: How is MTTF related to ROCOF in basic terms?
options: MTTF is unrelated to ROCOF always
MTTF is the reciprocal of ROCOF
MTTF is smaller when ROCOF is zero
MTTF is the sum of ROCOF values
MTTF is the square of ROCOF value
questions.explanation: Mean time to failure is the reciprocal of the failure rate in simple models.

questions.question: What is the core idea of N-version programming?
options: Run one version and ignore invalid inputs
Run one version and disable redundancy
Run one version and retry after failures
Run independent versions and vote on outputs
Run one version and log errors for later
questions.explanation: N-version programming uses multiple independently developed implementations and majority voting to tolerate faults.

questions.question: Triple Modular Redundancy (TMR) primarily relies on what mechanism?
options: Three replicas with majority vote output
Single replica with perfect formal proof
One replica with timeouts only
Multiple retries with random input reshaping
Two replicas with manual operator selection
questions.explanation: TMR uses three replicated components and uses majority voting to mask one faulty output.

questions.question: What is an operational profile in reliability testing?
options: Sequence of UML diagrams for architecture
Set of coding standards for a project
Distribution of inputs representing real usage
Schedule of sprint tasks for a release
List of defects found during unit testing
questions.explanation: An operational profile models how the system is actually used so reliability tests reflect real demand patterns.

questions.question: Which limitation is commonly associated with formal methods?
options: Perfect alignment with minimal project documentation
High cost and difficulty scaling to large systems
Guaranteed understanding by all nontechnical stakeholders
Elimination of need for all testing activities
Automatic correction of all specification errors always
questions.explanation: Formal methods can detect errors early, but they are expensive, hard to scale, and difficult for many stakeholders to use.

questions.question: Which set correctly lists the four core software process activities?
options: Specification, development, validation, evolution
Specification, deployment, operation, retirement
Planning, coding, debugging, publishing
Analysis, testing, marketing, maintenance
Design, coding, compiling, packaging
questions.explanation: Core activities are specifying needs, developing the system, validating it, and evolving it after delivery.

questions.question: Which statement best characterizes software engineering as a discipline?
options: It covers the full lifecycle of software systems
It focuses only on writing efficient algorithms
It replaces testing with developer intuition
It avoids process to maximize speed
It treats maintenance as out of scope
questions.explanation: Software engineering spans requirements, design, implementation, validation, and evolution.

questions.question: Which attribute most directly concerns ease of changing a system over time?
options: Maintainability
Portability
Novelty
Profitability
Popularity
questions.explanation: Maintainability is about how easily a system can be modified and evolved.

questions.question: Which attribute most directly concerns trust that services work correctly and safely?
options: Dependability and security
Aesthetic appeal
Feature density
Brand recognition
Algorithm novelty
questions.explanation: Dependability and security capture reliability, safety-related trust, and protection from threats.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects typical long-term cost distribution for major software systems?
options: Maintenance can exceed initial development cost
Development always exceeds maintenance cost
Hardware always dominates software cost
Licensing always dominates maintenance cost
Training always dominates development cost
questions.explanation: For long-lived systems, evolution and maintenance often cost more than initial development.

questions.question: Which system type most strongly emphasizes real-time constraints and safety risks?
options: Embedded control system
Batch processing system
Standalone desktop tool
Document management system
Entertainment media player
questions.explanation: Embedded control often interacts with the physical world and may require real-time and safety assurance.

questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes generic products from custom systems?
options: Generic products target a market; custom systems target one client
Generic products are always free; custom systems are always paid
Generic products avoid requirements; custom systems avoid testing
Generic products require no maintenance; custom systems require none
Generic products forbid reuse; custom systems mandate reuse
questions.explanation: Generic products are built for a broad market; custom systems are commissioned for a specific customer.

questions.question: Which professional issue most directly concerns respecting reuse obligations and ownership?
options: Intellectual property rights
User interface consistency
Runtime performance tuning
Database normalization
Network bandwidth planning
questions.explanation: Licenses and ownership are handled under intellectual property rights responsibilities.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a software process model?
options: It is an abstract description of a development process
It is a compiled program that builds the system
It is a test suite that proves correctness
It is a licensing rule for distribution
It is a database schema for requirements
questions.explanation: A process model is a simplified representation used to understand and plan development.

questions.question: Which process model most strongly assumes stable requirements and sequential phases?
options: Waterfall development
Incremental development
Reuse-oriented development
Continuous deployment
Exploratory prototyping
questions.explanation: Waterfall organizes work into staged phases that are costly to revisit after completion.

questions.question: Which is a typical weakness of strict waterfall approaches?
options: Late requirement changes become expensive to handle
Unit testing becomes impossible to perform
Documentation cannot be produced by the team
Integration becomes unnecessary by definition
User feedback becomes illegal to collect
questions.explanation: Waterfall handles change poorly once phases are signed off, causing major rework.

questions.question: Which is a common benefit of incremental development?
options: It reduces the cost of accommodating requirement change
It eliminates the need for integration testing
It guarantees complete requirements at the start
It prevents architectural erosion automatically
It removes the need for stakeholder feedback
questions.explanation: Incremental delivery supports change by adjusting future increments based on feedback.

questions.question: Which is a realistic risk of delivering increments without structural maintenance?
options: Architecture quality can degrade across releases
Security threats disappear due to fast iteration
All defects become visible in early increments
Costs always fall as the codebase grows
Requirements always stabilize after one release
questions.explanation: Without refactoring and architectural attention, incremental delivery can lead to erosion.

questions.question: Which statement best characterizes reuse-oriented development?
options: It emphasizes integrating and configuring existing components
It emphasizes rewriting all modules each release
It emphasizes avoiding requirements engineering entirely
It emphasizes postponing validation until final delivery
It emphasizes forbidding third-party dependencies
questions.explanation: Reuse-oriented development focuses on selecting, adapting, and integrating existing software assets.

questions.question: Which test level best matches checking the whole system against user needs?
options: Acceptance testing
Unit testing
Static analysis
Compiler optimization
Code formatting
questions.explanation: Acceptance testing evaluates the complete system against customer or user expectations.

questions.question: Why can reliability measurement not rely only on defect-testing data?
options: Defect tests often use inputs unlike real operational usage
Defect tests always require zero failures observed
Defect tests never depend on system specifications
Defect tests guarantee statistically valid estimates
Defect tests ignore performance and availability
questions.explanation: Reliability estimation needs inputs reflecting real usage frequencies, not mainly edge cases.

questions.question: Which statement best characterizes agile development practices?
options: They deliver working software in short iterative cycles
They avoid testing to increase delivery speed
They require complete requirements before any coding
They forbid architecture decisions until the end
They guarantee zero changes after the first release
questions.explanation: Agile emphasizes iterative delivery with frequent feedback and continuous improvement.

questions.question: Which statement best defines refactoring?
options: It improves code structure without changing behavior
It adds new features without updating tests
It replaces requirements with user interviews
It converts UML diagrams into final binaries
It removes validation to reduce overhead
questions.explanation: Refactoring is internal restructuring that preserves externally visible behavior.

questions.question: Which practice best matches test-driven development?
options: Write a failing test, then implement to pass it
Write full code, then guess expected results
Skip unit tests, then run only acceptance tests
Write documentation, then delay tests to release
Write tests only after customers report bugs
questions.explanation: TDD starts with tests that define behavior, then code is written to satisfy them.

questions.question: Which role most directly protects the team from external disruptions in Scrum?
options: Scrum Master
Product Owner
System Administrator
Chief Financial Officer
Database Operator
questions.explanation: The Scrum Master facilitates the process and helps shield the team from interruptions.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a sprint outcome?
options: A working increment of the product is produced
A complete system specification is finalized
A full certification package is always approved
A final architecture is frozen permanently
A test suite is discarded and rewritten monthly
questions.explanation: Each sprint aims to deliver a potentially shippable increment.

questions.question: Why can large-scale agile development become difficult?
options: Cross-team coordination and dependencies increase sharply
Unit testing becomes impossible with many developers
Requirements stop changing when teams grow
Documentation becomes illegal under agile methods
Integration disappears when iterations are short
questions.explanation: Coordination overhead and shared architecture constraints grow with system and team size.

questions.question: Which statement best fits a user story?
options: A brief description of a user goal and value
A complete formal proof of correctness
A detailed data schema for every table
A fixed contract clause banning scope change
A low-level algorithm for a sorting function
questions.explanation: User stories capture small slices of value from the user's perspective.

questions.question: Which statement best explains why architectural refactoring can be costly?
options: It affects many components and cross-cutting dependencies
It affects only user interface colors and fonts
It affects only comments and formatting rules
It affects only a single isolated function
It affects only database indexes and keys
questions.explanation: Architecture changes ripple across many modules and interfaces, making rework broad.

questions.question: Which statement best defines functional requirements?
options: They specify services and behaviors the system must provide
They specify programming languages the team must use
They specify hiring plans for the development team
They specify marketing targets for product launch
They specify office policies for stakeholder meetings
questions.explanation: Functional requirements describe what the system should do.

questions.question: Which statement best defines non-functional requirements?
options: They constrain qualities such as performance and security
They list all user actions in a use case
They describe class attributes and associations
They define compiler settings for builds
They state variable naming conventions only
questions.explanation: Non-functional requirements define quality attributes and constraints on the system.

questions.question: Which pairing best distinguishes user and system requirements?
options: User requirements are readable; system requirements are detailed
User requirements are executable; system requirements are informal
User requirements are optional; system requirements are optional
User requirements are code; system requirements are sketches
User requirements are tests; system requirements are comments
questions.explanation: User requirements are high-level and understandable; system requirements are precise and detailed.

questions.question: Which set lists common checks used in requirements validation?
options: Validity, consistency, completeness, realism, verifiability
Popularity, novelty, aesthetics, speed, profitability
Inheritance, polymorphism, encapsulation, casting, overriding
Caching, routing, sharding, indexing, replication
Soldering, polishing, welding, molding, painting
questions.explanation: Validation checks whether requirements are correct, consistent, complete, realistic, and testable.

questions.question: Which activity most directly resolves stakeholder conflicts about requirements?
options: Negotiation and prioritization
Code optimization and profiling
Database indexing and partitioning
Memory allocation and garbage collection
Compiler linking and packaging
questions.explanation: Conflicting needs are resolved by negotiating trade-offs and setting priorities.

questions.question: Which change-management step most directly evaluates impact and cost?
options: Change analysis and costing
Change implementation and deployment
Change marketing and promotion
Change denial and archiving
Change coding and formatting
questions.explanation: Impact analysis estimates what must change and how expensive the change will be.

questions.question: Why can non-functional requirements be difficult to assign to a single feature?
options: They often emerge from the whole system design
They apply only to single functions by definition
They always depend on compiler flags only
They never affect architecture decisions
They remove the need for system testing
questions.explanation: Quality attributes like performance and security depend on system-wide structure and interactions.

questions.question: Which statement best explains why requirements change is common?
options: Business context and technical understanding evolve over time
All requirements are complete at project start
Stakeholders never revise priorities after approval
New systems always copy identical older systems
Testing automatically prevents requirement change
questions.explanation: Organizations, constraints, and understanding change, so requirements must be managed as evolving artifacts.

questions.question: Which model best represents a system boundary and its external environment?
options: A context model
A class model
A state model
A timing model
A compiler model
questions.explanation: Context models show system boundaries and interactions with external systems.

questions.question: Which UML diagram best shows actor goals and high-level interactions?
options: A use case diagram
A class diagram
A state diagram
A package diagram
A deployment diagram
questions.explanation: Use case diagrams summarize actor interactions with the system boundary.

questions.question: Which UML diagram best shows message ordering over time in a scenario?
options: A sequence diagram
A class diagram
A package diagram
A context diagram
A data dictionary
questions.explanation: Sequence diagrams add temporal ordering of interactions between objects.

questions.question: Which UML diagram best represents static structure of classes and associations?
options: A class diagram
A sequence diagram
A state diagram
A use case diagram
A timing diagram
questions.explanation: Class diagrams describe classes and their static relationships.

questions.question: Which UML diagram best represents event-driven state changes of an object?
options: A state diagram
A class diagram
A use case diagram
A package diagram
A context diagram
questions.explanation: State diagrams show states and transitions triggered by events.

questions.question: Which statement best explains why state diagrams are not required for every object?
options: Only objects with meaningful states need state modeling
All objects must have state diagrams by UML rule
State diagrams replace requirements documents entirely
State diagrams are used only for database tables
State diagrams guarantee correctness without testing
questions.explanation: State modeling is useful when an object's behavior changes significantly across states.

questions.question: Which statement best characterizes model-driven engineering?
options: Models are primary artifacts and code may be generated
Source code is primary artifact and models are forbidden
Models replace validation and testing entirely
Models eliminate the need for requirements engineering
Models guarantee correct performance on all platforms
questions.explanation: MDE treats models as central artifacts, sometimes generating code via transformations.

questions.question: Which is a realistic limitation of heavy up-front modeling adoption?
options: Tooling and transformations can require specialized support
Models cannot represent any system context at all
UML cannot represent classes and relationships
Code generation makes integration unnecessary
Operational profiles become irrelevant to testing
questions.explanation: MDE often depends on tooling and can conflict with lightweight iterative approaches.

questions.question: Which statement best defines software architecture?
options: It describes major components and their interactions
It describes variable names and formatting rules
It describes compiler flags and link options
It describes only database table definitions
It describes only unit test case lists
questions.explanation: Architecture captures the high-level structure and communication among system components.

questions.question: In the 4+1 model, which view focuses on interacting runtime processes?
options: Process view
Logical view
Development view
Physical view
Contract view
questions.explanation: The process view describes how the system is composed of runtime processes and their interactions.

questions.question: Which architectural pattern best fits subsystems sharing large data via a central store?
options: Repository architecture
Layered architecture
Client-server architecture
Pipe-and-filter architecture
Peer-to-peer architecture
questions.explanation: Repository architectures centralize shared data to support efficient exchange.

questions.question: Which architectural choice most directly supports security by isolating critical assets?
options: Layered design with critical assets in inner layers
Pipe-and-filter design for interactive user workflows
Repository design with unrestricted global access
Single-tier design with shared global state
Monolithic design without any access boundaries
questions.explanation: Layered architectures can place sensitive components deeper with controlled access paths.

questions.question: Which pattern best matches batch transformations applied in a fixed sequence?
options: Pipe-and-filter architecture
Client-server architecture
Repository architecture
MVC architecture
Layered architecture
questions.explanation: Pipe-and-filter fits staged data transformations typical in batch pipelines.

questions.question: Which statement best explains why box-and-line diagrams can be risky as specifications?
options: They can lack precise semantics without defined notation rules
They always include mathematically complete proofs
They always eliminate the need for requirements work
They always prevent architectural misunderstanding
They always guarantee correct performance outcomes
questions.explanation: Informal diagrams may be interpreted differently unless their notation and meaning are fixed.

questions.question: Which component order best matches a typical compiler pipeline stage early on?
options: Lexical analysis before syntax analysis
Code generation before lexical analysis
Optimization before syntax analysis
Linking before semantic analysis
Deployment before parsing
questions.explanation: Compilers typically tokenize input (lexical analysis) before building syntax structure (parsing).

questions.question: Which statement best explains why architectural refactoring is often costly?
options: It can require coordinated changes across many components
It can require only renaming local variables
It can require only updating code comments
It can require only changing UI colors
It can require only reordering import statements
questions.explanation: Architecture affects many modules and interfaces, so changes tend to ripple widely.

questions.question: A design pattern description typically includes which set of elements?
options: Name, problem, solution, consequences
Name, compiler, license, build flags
Actors, states, transitions, events
Inputs, outputs, throughput, latency
Tables, keys, indexes, triggers
questions.explanation: Patterns are documented with a name, the problem, the solution structure, and trade-offs.

questions.question: Which statement best describes build-or-buy impacts on design work?
options: It shifts focus toward configuring features to meet requirements
It shifts focus toward eliminating stakeholder communication
It shifts focus toward avoiding modeling entirely
It shifts focus toward proving full correctness formally
It shifts focus toward ignoring non-functional constraints
questions.explanation: With COTS, the key work is matching needs to existing capabilities and configuring integration.

questions.question: Which statement best describes abstraction-level reuse?
options: It reuses successful design ideas and abstractions
It reuses entire enterprise systems unchanged
It reuses only database engines and schemas
It reuses only one object from a library
It reuses only compiler-generated code
questions.explanation: Abstraction reuse means applying proven concepts and designs, not copying entire systems.

questions.question: Which activity most directly belongs to configuration management?
options: Controlling versions and tracking component changes
Selecting colors and fonts for user interfaces
Choosing office policies for team meetings
Forecasting market share for product launches
Designing electrical circuits for device power
questions.explanation: Configuration management coordinates versions, builds, and controlled changes in evolving systems.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the purpose of interface specification?
options: It defines how a component is used without revealing internals
It defines how a compiler optimizes generated machine code
It defines how to remove all tests from a release
It defines how to skip requirements negotiation
It defines how to replace architecture with diagrams
questions.explanation: Interfaces provide stable contracts and hide representation details for safe component use.

questions.question: Which statement best describes system-level reuse?
options: It reuses an entire application system in a new context
It reuses one method from a utility library
It reuses one database index definition
It reuses one variable naming convention
It reuses one unit test assertion line
questions.explanation: System reuse adopts whole systems (often configurable) rather than individual objects or components.

questions.question: Which statement best characterizes open-source licensing impact on reuse?
options: It can impose obligations on redistribution of derived works
It guarantees unlimited proprietary distribution rights
It eliminates any need to track third-party components
It forbids any modification of the original code
It prevents any commercial usage of the code
questions.explanation: Some licenses (e.g., copyleft) require sharing source or preserving license terms in derivatives.

questions.question: Which statement best describes host-target development?
options: Development occurs on one platform and execution occurs on another
Development and execution always occur on identical hardware
Development occurs only in production environments
Execution occurs only inside the compiler toolchain
Development occurs only without any external libraries
questions.explanation: Code is built on a host system and deployed to a target system with different constraints.

questions.question: Which statement best defines system dependability?
options: It reflects trust that services are delivered as expected
It reflects number of features delivered each sprint
It reflects amount of code written per week
It reflects maximum CPU usage under load
It reflects popularity in app store rankings
questions.explanation: Dependability is about trust in correct, reliable, and safe service delivery.

questions.question: Which set lists major dependability-related attributes?
options: Availability, reliability, safety, security, resilience
Speed, novelty, branding, aesthetics, trendiness
Caching, routing, sharding, indexing, replication
Inheritance, polymorphism, encapsulation, casting, overloading
Parsing, linking, packaging, installing, theming
questions.explanation: Dependability includes being available, reliable, safe, secure, and able to recover under disruption.

questions.question: In socio-technical systems, which cause often dominates system failures?
options: Operational mistakes made by humans during use
Perfect hardware manufacturing with no variation
Compiler optimization causing all runtime crashes
Encryption preventing any system state changes
Redundancy automatically removing all faults
questions.explanation: Human operational errors are a major failure source in complex socio-technical settings.

questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes redundancy from diversity?
options: Redundancy adds backups; diversity varies implementations
Redundancy varies implementations; diversity adds backups
Redundancy forbids change; diversity forbids planning
Redundancy means no testing; diversity means more testing
Redundancy applies only to software; diversity applies only to hardware
questions.explanation: Redundancy duplicates components; diversity reduces common-mode failures via different implementations.

questions.question: Which statement best explains why pure agile is often impractical for dependable systems work?
options: Certification needs evidence and documentation beyond minimal artifacts
Iterative development is forbidden by agile methods
Verification and validation are banned by agile methods
Dependable systems cannot be tested realistically
Requirements never change in dependable systems
questions.explanation: Regulated or critical systems require documented assurance evidence, not only working increments.

questions.question: Which statement best characterizes a socio-technical system?
options: It combines software, hardware, people, and organizational processes
It contains only source code and test cases
It contains only hardware components and sensors
It contains only database records and schemas
It contains only web services and APIs
questions.explanation: Socio-technical systems include technology and the human/organizational context that operates it.

questions.question: Which statement best describes resilience in critical systems?
options: It sustains or restores service under disruption or attack
It maximizes user interface animations under load
It ensures requirements never change after approval
It guarantees failures never occur in any component
It eliminates need for monitoring and recovery
questions.explanation: Resilience emphasizes continued operation and recovery rather than complete failure prevention.

questions.question: Which statement best describes formal methods in dependability contexts?
options: They use precise specifications to reduce certain defect classes
They remove the need for requirements engineering
They guarantee absence of accidents in socio-technical systems
They replace all testing with customer interviews
They make operational profiles irrelevant to reliability
questions.explanation: Formal methods can increase assurance by proving properties, but do not eliminate all risks.

questions.question: Which chain best matches fault, error, and failure relationships?
options: A fault may cause an error; an error may cause a failure
A failure may cause an error; an error may cause a fault
A fault always causes a failure; failure always causes error
An error always causes a fault; fault always causes failure
A failure always causes a fault; fault always causes error
questions.explanation: Faults can create erroneous states, and errors can propagate into observable failures, but not always.

questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes reliability from availability?
options: Reliability is failure-free over time; availability is up at a point in time
Reliability is up at a point in time; availability is failure-free over time
Reliability is subjective only; availability is objective only
Reliability equals uptime only; availability equals correctness only
Reliability equals security only; availability equals privacy only
questions.explanation: Reliability is about continuous correct operation; availability includes uptime and recovery at a moment.

questions.question: Which metric best fits rare and intermittent demands such as emergency shutdown?
options: Probability of failure on demand (POFOD)
Rate of occurrence of failures (ROCOF)
Mean time to repair (MTTR)
Availability fraction only
Defect density per module
questions.explanation: POFOD measures failure probability when a demand occurs, matching intermittent-demand services.

questions.question: Which metric best fits high-volume transaction processing systems?
options: Rate of occurrence of failures (ROCOF)
Probability of failure on demand (POFOD)
Availability fraction only
Mean time to install (MTTI)
Lines of code per feature
questions.explanation: ROCOF measures failure rate per time unit in systems handling many similar requests.

questions.question: Which statement best explains why reliability testing needs special test data?
options: Operational profiles require inputs distributed like real usage
Reliability testing ignores specifications by design
Reliability testing requires zero failures by definition
Reliability testing uses only formal proofs for evidence
Reliability testing depends only on code coverage values
questions.explanation: Reliability estimates depend on usage frequency, so test inputs must reflect operational distributions.

questions.question: Which architecture best matches an independent emergency protection mechanism?
options: A protection system that monitors and can trigger shutdown
A repository system that centralizes shared data
A pipe-and-filter system that chains transformations
A layered system that separates presentation from domain
A client-server system that serves browser requests
questions.explanation: Protection systems independently monitor and take emergency action to avoid catastrophe.

questions.question: Which statement best describes N-version programming?
options: Multiple independent versions vote on a computed result
One optimized version replaces all other components
One version runs faster by skipping validation
Multiple versions share one identical codebase
Multiple versions remove need for specifications
questions.explanation: N-version uses diverse implementations and voting to reduce impact of individual faults.

questions.question: Which statement best characterizes a key problem with software diversity?
options: Teams can share the same specification misunderstandings
Teams always produce independent errors by default
Teams always choose different algorithms by policy
Teams always eliminate common-mode failures completely
Teams always reduce development cost below baseline
questions.explanation: Common spec errors and shared interpretations can cause correlated failures across versions.

questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes safety from reliability?
options: Safety concerns harm risk; reliability concerns failure-free operation
Safety concerns uptime; reliability concerns user satisfaction
Safety concerns speed; reliability concerns code style
Safety concerns UI design; reliability concerns licensing
Safety concerns cost; reliability concerns team size
questions.explanation: Safety is about preventing unacceptable harm, while reliability is about failure-free service delivery.

questions.question: Which statement best defines a hazard?
options: A condition that could lead to an accident
A confirmed accident with recorded damage
A unit test that fails during execution
A performance bottleneck under heavy load
A documentation gap in a design review
questions.explanation: A hazard is a potential source of harm, not the harm event itself.

questions.question: Which option best describes ALARP risk treatment?
options: Reduce risk as far as reasonably practicable
Accept risk whenever testing is expensive
Ignore risk once uptime exceeds a target
Eliminate risk by forbidding all software change
Maximize risk to accelerate delivery speed
questions.explanation: ALARP means lowering risk until further reduction is not reasonably justified.

questions.question: Which technique is deductive and top-down in safety analysis?
options: Fault-tree analysis starting from an accident
Code review starting from style guidelines
Unit testing starting from one function
User interview starting from preferences
Benchmarking starting from latency targets
questions.explanation: Fault-tree analysis begins with a hazardous outcome and decomposes causes using logic.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a safety case?
options: A structured argument with evidence for acceptable safety
A marketing claim that safety is guaranteed
A bug list showing only closed issues
A source code archive stored for auditing
A performance report for peak throughput
questions.explanation: Safety cases present claims, arguments, and evidence that hazards are controlled adequately.

questions.question: Why are some safety requirements written as prohibitions?
options: They forbid unsafe states and unsafe events explicitly
They make validation unnecessary by definition
They guarantee reliability without redundancy
They replace hazard analysis with checklists
They prevent any need for operator training
questions.explanation: Safety requirements often specify what must never happen to avoid hazardous situations.

questions.question: Which statement best characterizes static analysis in safety assurance?
options: It examines code for defects without executing it
It proves all hazards are impossible in practice
It replaces all dynamic testing by definition
It estimates reliability using operational profiles
It generates new requirements automatically
questions.explanation: Static analysis checks properties of code without running it, catching certain fault classes early.

questions.question: Which statement best characterizes model checking in safety-critical contexts?
options: It explores system states to find violations of properties
It guarantees correctness for any real-world environment
It eliminates need for specifications and models
It measures availability by counting repair minutes
It improves performance by optimizing binaries
questions.explanation: Model checking systematically explores states of a model to detect property violations and deadlocks.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the essential attributes of good software?
options: Maintainability
Dependability and security
Scalability
Acceptability
questions.explanation: The essential attributes listed are maintainability, dependability/security, efficiency, and acceptability; scalability is not in that set.

questions.question: A company develops a software system for internal use and controls all changes. This is an example of:
options: A generic product
A customized product
An open source product
A COTS product
questions.explanation: Generic products are owned and evolved by the developing organization, which controls the specification and changes.

questions.question: The principle stating engineers act in clients' and employers' interests consistent with the public interest is:
options: PUBLIC
PRODUCT
CLIENT AND EMPLOYER
JUDGMENT
questions.explanation: That statement matches the 'Client and Employer' principle while requiring consistency with public interest.

questions.question: What does the principle of competence in software engineering ethics require?
options: Always use the latest technology
Not misrepresent competence or accept work outside it
Have a university degree
Work overtime to meet deadlines
questions.explanation: Competence requires truthful representation of skills and avoiding work beyond one’s ability.

questions.question: In which process model are specification, development, and validation interleaved with frequent releases?
options: Waterfall model
Incremental development
Integration and configuration
V-model
questions.explanation: Incremental development delivers working software in repeated increments with interleaved activities.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of incremental development compared to waterfall?
options: It requires less testing
It produces more documentation
It reduces cost of accommodating changing requirements
It is easier to manage large distributed teams
questions.explanation: Incremental delivery makes late requirement changes cheaper by deferring changes into later increments.

questions.question: Which is an example of a reusable software type in integration and configuration?
options: User requirements document
Waterfall model phases
Web services developed according to service standards
Unit test cases
questions.explanation: Reuse-oriented development commonly integrates reusable services/components such as standardized web services.

questions.question: What is the purpose of system prototyping?
options: Replace the final system
Demonstrate concepts and help with requirements elicitation
Generate automatic documentation
Measure the system's reliability
questions.explanation: Prototypes explore feasibility and clarify requirements by trying ideas early.

questions.question: Which is one of the four values of the Agile Manifesto?
options: Processes and tools over individuals and interactions
Comprehensive documentation over working software
Contract negotiation over customer collaboration
Responding to change over following a plan
questions.explanation: Agile values responding to change over strict adherence to a plan.

questions.question: In Extreme Programming (XP), what are user stories?
options: Detailed technical specifications
Short scenario requirements written on cards
UML diagrams showing user interactions
Bug reports from users
questions.explanation: User stories are brief scenarios capturing requirements from a user perspective.

questions.question: What is the role of the Scrum Master?
options: Write all the code for the team
Facilitate, protect the team from distractions, remove impediments
Manage the backlog and prioritize features
Test the software at the end of each sprint
questions.explanation: The Scrum Master supports the process and removes blockers so the team can deliver.

questions.question: Which is a problem with scaling agile methods to large systems?
options: Agile methods require too much documentation
Large systems may require up-front design and face external regulations
Agile teams cannot have more than 5 people
Large systems cannot be tested
questions.explanation: Large/regulated systems often need more up-front analysis and assurance evidence than pure agile assumes.

questions.question: A requirement stating the system shall generate a daily patient appointment list is a:
options: Non-functional requirement
Functional requirement
Domain requirement
Organizational requirement
questions.explanation: It specifies a service the system must provide, which is functional.

questions.question: A requirement stating the system shall be available 99.9% between 8am and 8pm is a:
options: Functional requirement
Verifiable non-functional requirement
Goal
Domain requirement
questions.explanation: Availability is a quality attribute with a measurable target, so it is a verifiable non-functional requirement.

questions.question: Which elicitation technique is best for understanding actual work practices including social factors?
options: Interviewing
Questionnaire
Ethnography
Brainstorming
questions.explanation: Ethnography observes real work to uncover tacit and social/organizational practices.

questions.question: Requirements validation checks all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Validity
Consistency
Completeness
Profitability
questions.explanation: Validation focuses on correctness/quality of requirements, not business profitability.

questions.question: Which UML diagram shows static structure including classes, attributes, and associations?
options: Sequence diagram
Use case diagram
Class diagram
State diagram
questions.explanation: Class diagrams represent static structure and relationships.

questions.question: In a class diagram, what does generalization represent?
options: A has-a relationship
An is-a relationship
A uses relationship
A temporal relationship
questions.explanation: Generalization indicates inheritance (is-a).

questions.question: Which UML diagram best models how a microwave responds to button presses and changes internal state?
options: Activity diagram
Sequence diagram
Use case diagram
State diagram
questions.explanation: State diagrams model event-driven state transitions.

questions.question: In Model-Driven Architecture (MDA), what is a Platform Independent Model (PIM)?
options: A model of the business domain
A model describing operation without reference to platform
A model specific to Java or .NET
A model of the hardware architecture
questions.explanation: A PIM abstracts the system’s behavior independently of a specific technology platform.

questions.question: Which architectural pattern fits components processing data and passing results along a sequence?
options: Repository pattern
Client-server
Pipe-and-filter
Layered architecture
questions.explanation: Pipe-and-filter structures computation as a chain of processing stages.

questions.question: In the 4+1 view model, which view shows key abstractions as objects or object classes?
options: Logical view
Process view
Development view
Physical view
questions.explanation: The logical view captures major abstractions and relationships.

questions.question: To achieve high performance, which architectural strategy is recommended?
options: Use fine-grain components with frequent communication
Localize critical operations and minimize communications
Put all components on separate servers
Use a single layer for all functionality
questions.explanation: Performance improves when you reduce inter-component communication and keep critical work localized.

questions.question: Which pattern uses a central data structure accessed and updated by all components?
options: MVC
Pipe-and-filter
Layered
Repository
questions.explanation: Repository architectures center shared data in one store.

questions.question: Which is NOT a common activity in an object-oriented design process?
options: Define context and modes of use
Design the system architecture
Write all code before creating any models
Specify object interfaces
questions.explanation: OO design typically uses models/interfaces before or alongside coding, not coding everything first.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the Observer design pattern?
options: Provide a simplified interface to a complex subsystem
Separate state from displays and allow multiple displays
Allow an object to alter behavior when internal state changes
Encapsulate a request as an object
questions.explanation: Observer decouples a subject from multiple observers that update when the subject changes.

questions.question: At which reuse level do you directly reuse objects from a library?
options: Abstraction level
Object level
Component level
System level
questions.explanation: Object-level reuse means using library objects/classes directly.

questions.question: Which open source license is reciprocal and requires derived software to be open source?
options: BSD License
MIT License
GNU General Public License (GPL)
Apache License
questions.explanation: GPL is a copyleft license requiring redistribution of derivatives under similar terms.

questions.question: Which dependability property is a judgment of likelihood the system will cause damage to people or environment?
options: Reliability
Availability
Safety
Security
questions.explanation: Safety concerns risk of harm and accidents.

questions.question: What is the relationship between reliability and safety?
options: A reliable system is always safe
A safe system is always reliable
Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for safety
They are completely unrelated
questions.explanation: Reliability helps, but safety also depends on hazards, context, and preventing unacceptable harm.

questions.question: What is the purpose of diversity in dependable systems?
options: Provide backup copies of components
Implement the same function differently to avoid common-mode failures
Make the system more complex
Reduce development costs
questions.explanation: Diversity aims to prevent the same fault from causing simultaneous failures across replicas.

questions.question: What is the main benefit of formal methods in dependable systems engineering?
options: They are easy for customers to understand
They reduce certain programming errors and can find specification errors
They are cheaper than testing
They work well with agile methods
questions.explanation: Formal methods provide precise specifications and analysis that can expose spec/design defects and certain code errors.

questions.question: If code contains a fault but that part is never executed, what is the result?
options: An error will occur
A failure will occur
No error or failure necessarily occurs
The system will crash immediately
questions.explanation: A fault only causes errors/failures if it is activated (executed under relevant conditions).

questions.question: For a credit card processing system handling millions of transactions per day, which metric is most appropriate?
options: POFOD
ROCOF
AVAIL
MTTF
questions.explanation: High transaction-rate systems are best assessed by failure rate over time (ROCOF).

questions.question: What is an operational profile in reliability testing?
options: A profile of development team members
Test data with frequencies matching normal usage inputs
A document describing system operation
A diagram showing system states
questions.explanation: Operational profiles reflect real input distributions so reliability estimates match real-world use.

questions.question: Which practice is recommended for dependable programming?
options: Use goto for complex logic
Use unbounded arrays for flexibility
Check all inputs for validity and reasonableness
Avoid exception handlers to keep code simple
questions.explanation: Input validation (range/size/representation/reasonableness) prevents many failures and security issues.

questions.question: What is the key insight of normal accidents theory in complex systems?
options: Accidents always have a single cause
Single-point failure design is sufficient
Accidents usually result from combinations of malfunctions
Software failures cannot cause accidents
questions.explanation: In complex systems, accidents often emerge from interacting failures rather than a single isolated cause.

questions.question: In hazard assessment, what does ALARP stand for?
options: A Little Additional Risk is Permitted
As Low As Reasonably Practicable
Always Look for Additional Risk Patterns
A Legal Assessment of Risk Protection
questions.explanation: ALARP means reducing risk to the lowest level that is reasonably practicable.

questions.question: Fault-tree analysis (FTA) is best described as:
options: An inductive bottom-up technique starting from failures
A deductive top-down technique starting from hazards
A type of statistical testing
A code review technique
questions.explanation: FTA starts with a hazard/accident and decomposes causes using logic (AND/OR).

questions.question: What is the purpose of a safety case?
options: Prove the software has no bugs
Provide a structured argument with evidence of adequate safety
Replace all other documentation
Insure the company against accidents
questions.explanation: A safety case is an evidence-based justification that risks are controlled to an acceptable level.

questions.question: A design pattern description typically includes which set of elements?
options: Name, problem, solution, consequences
Name, code, compiler version, license
Actors, states, transitions, events
Inputs, outputs, throughput, latency
questions.explanation: Design patterns are documented by naming the pattern, stating the problem, describing the solution structure, and listing consequences/trade-offs.

questions.question: Why is “pure agile” often impractical for dependable systems engineering?
options: Dependable systems cannot be tested
Agile cannot use iterative development
Certification needs process/product documentation and upfront requirements analysis; agile minimizes documentation and interleaves specs with code
Agile bans verification and validation
questions.explanation: Regulated dependable systems require evidence, documentation, and upfront analysis that pure agile typically de-emphasizes.

questions.question: In the 4 + 1 view model, which view focuses on how the system is composed of interacting processes at run-time?
options: Logical view
Development view
Process view
Physical view
questions.explanation: The process view describes run-time processes/threads and how they interact.

questions.question: Which is a realistic reason MDA/MDE adoption can be limited (and makes “agile + MDA” tricky)?
options: Models cannot represent system context
Transformations require specialized tool support and extensive up-front modeling can conflict with agile values
MDA eliminates the need for requirements engineering
UML does not support class diagrams
questions.explanation: MDA/MDE can demand heavy upfront modeling and specialized transformation tooling, which can clash with lightweight iterative practices.

questions.question: Which architectural choice most directly aligns with security guidance?
options: Prefer pipe-and-filter for interactive systems
Use fine-grain replaceable components for all modules
Prefer box-and-line diagrams because they have precise semantics
Use layered architecture with critical assets in inner layers
questions.explanation: Layering helps isolate critical assets in inner layers and control access paths, supporting security.

questions.question: Which chain is most consistent with fault, error, and failure terminology?
options: Fault leads to failure and then error
Fault may lead to error; error may lead to failure
Failure may lead to fault; fault may lead to error
Error leads to fault and then failure
questions.explanation: A fault can cause an erroneous state, and an error can propagate into an externally visible failure, but not always.

questions.question: In early-stage requirements discussions, which statement best matches the intended use of graphical models?
options: Only behavioral models are useful; structural models confuse stakeholders
Models must be complete and correct because they will be used to generate code
Models should avoid UML because UML is only for implementation
Incomplete or incorrect models can be acceptable if they facilitate stakeholder discussion
questions.explanation: Early models are often used to communicate and explore, so they can be partial as long as they support discussion.

questions.question: Which UML model is best suited to show how an object changes state in response to events?
options: Use case diagram
Package diagram
Class diagram
State diagram
questions.explanation: State diagrams capture event-driven transitions between states for an object.

questions.question: In socio-technical systems, which factor is often the largest single cause of system failures?
options: Operational failure due to human mistakes
Hardware reaching end-of-life
Software specification errors
Lack of formal methods
questions.explanation: Human operational errors frequently dominate failures in socio-technical contexts.

questions.question: “Build or buy” (COTS) most directly changes the main concern of design into which focus?
options: Deciding how to use configuration features to meet requirements
Eliminating stakeholder communication
Avoiding UML models entirely
Proving program correctness formally
questions.explanation: With COTS, design effort shifts toward selecting and configuring existing capabilities to satisfy requirements.

questions.question: Which pairing best matches context modeling and interaction modeling?
options: Context model is behavioral; interaction model is structural
Context model is data-driven; interaction model is event-driven
Context model is structural; interaction model is dynamic
Context model is dynamic; interaction model is structural
questions.explanation: Context models describe structure around the system boundary; interaction models describe dynamic usage/interactions.

questions.question: Why cannot statistical reliability testing data simply reuse normal defect-testing data?
options: Reliability testing ignores specifications
Defect testing data is usually atypical of real operational usage patterns
Defect testing always uses formal proofs
Reliability testing requires no failures at all
questions.explanation: Reliability estimates require input frequencies matching operational profiles; defect tests often overuse edge cases.

questions.question: Which dependability property is defined as probability the system will be up and running and able to deliver useful services?
options: Safety
Availability
Resilience
Reliability
questions.explanation: Availability measures the likelihood the system is operational and can deliver service at a point in time.

questions.question: Why can refactoring the architecture be especially expensive in agile projects?
options: It is cheaper than refactoring code
It only affects UI components
It is prohibited by UML
It affects many components and cross-cutting dependencies
questions.explanation: Architectural changes ripple across interfaces and components, increasing coordination and rework cost.

questions.question: Which statement about reuse levels is correct?
options: Object-level reuse means only reusing databases
Component-level reuse means reusing entire application systems
Abstraction-level reuse means reusing knowledge of successful abstractions in design
System-level reuse means reusing a single object from a library
questions.explanation: Abstraction-level reuse reuses proven design concepts and abstractions, not just code artifacts.

questions.question: Which statement best distinguishes reliability from availability?
options: Reliability is probability of failure-free operation over time; availability is probability system is operational at a point in time
Both mean the same thing in critical systems
Reliability is subjective; availability is always subjective
Reliability is up-time; availability is failure-free operation
questions.explanation: Reliability concerns failure-free behavior over an interval; availability concerns being operational now (including repair/recovery).

questions.question: Which option best captures the difference between redundancy and diversity for dependability improvement?
options: Both mean more testing
Diversity applies only to hardware; redundancy applies only to software
Redundancy adds backup components; diversity uses different implementations to reduce common-mode failures
Redundancy uses different implementations; diversity adds a backup copy
questions.explanation: Redundancy duplicates capability; diversity reduces correlated failures by implementing the same function differently.

questions.question: Subsystems exchanging large amounts of shared data via a central store most precisely describes which pattern?
options: Layered architecture
Client-server architecture
Pipe-and-filter architecture
Repository architecture
questions.explanation: Repository architectures centralize data so subsystems can share it efficiently through a common store.

questions.question: A system with intermittent and infrequent demands (e.g., emergency shutdown) is best assessed using which metric?
options: MTTF
Availability only
POFOD
ROCOF
questions.explanation: For rare-demand functions, probability of failure on demand (POFOD) best captures risk when the demand occurs.

questions.question: A sequence diagram adds which information beyond a use-case overview?
options: Hardware deployment nodes and network topology
A list of system stakeholders and constraints
Object-to-object interaction ordering over time for a scenario instance
Static class attributes and associations
questions.explanation: Sequence diagrams show the time-ordered message flow among objects for a particular scenario.
